# Discount Governance

Source: https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Discount governance is the set of rules that decides who may offer what discount, in exchange for what, and how the decision is recorded. It matters because price changes have outsized effects on profit: the classic Harvard Business Review analysis found that a 1% improvement in realised price lifted operating profit by 11.1% for an average large firm, against 3.3% for a 1% rise in volume. Most firms govern discounts with an approval chain and nothing else, which slows deals without teaching anyone anything. A working system sets discount bands, attaches a trade to every concession, rules within a stated time and records the reason, so that the pattern of exceptions can be reviewed and the bands improved.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Across 2,463 companies, a 1% improvement in realised price lifted operating profit by 11.1%, against 7.8% for a 1% cut in variable cost and 3.3% for a 1% rise in volume.
- McKinsey's 2026 analysis of 140 public distributors found a 1% price increase could lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%, and one distributor's sellers overrode system prices in more than half of transactions.
- In a 2026 vendor survey of 195 revenue leaders, 47% said their teams took three days or more to approve a pricing exception.
- Benchmark data suggests early discounting lowers win rates, because it signals that the price was never the real price.
- Every approved exception is a decision with a reason, owner and expected outcome, and a quarter of them shows where the bands are wrong.

Discounting is one of the most frequent commercial decisions a firm makes, and one of the least examined. A seller asks for 15% to close by quarter end. A manager approves it because the forecast needs the deal. Nobody records why, and nobody checks a year later whether the customer renewed at the discounted price or the list price.

Part 4 of this series covered pricing architecture: how list prices, packages and terms are set. This piece covers what happens after: how a firm decides, deal by deal, how far to move from the price it set. The explainer on [deal desks](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-deal-desk/) covers the team that often runs this process; this piece covers the rules it runs.

## Why small discounts matter more than they look

The arithmetic is old and still decisive. In "Managing Price, Gaining Profit", published in Harvard Business Review in 1992, Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello used the average economics of 2,463 companies in the Compustat database to compare profit levers. A 1% improvement in price, with volume held steady, lifted operating profit by 11.1%. A 1% cut in variable cost lifted it by 7.8%, and a 1% rise in volume by 3.3%. The same arithmetic runs in reverse: a 1% average discount gives up about 11% of operating profit.

The effect is stronger where margins are thin. McKinsey's July 2026 analysis of 10-K filings from 140 public distributors found that a 1% price increase could lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%.

Marn and Rosiello also showed why firms underestimate the leak. They traced the "pocket price waterfall", the fall from list price to invoice price to the revenue actually kept once payment terms, volume rebates, promotional allowances and freight were taken off. In their examples the drop from invoice price to pocket price ranged from 16.7% in consumer packaged goods to 28.9% in lighting products. For a single product at similar volumes, the range of pocket prices customers actually paid ran from 35% in one case to 500% in another. Most of that variation was not a decision anyone had made. It was the sum of exceptions granted one at a time.

Services and software firms have fewer off-invoice items, but they have their own: free implementation days, extended payment terms, uncapped usage, multi-year price locks and early renewal credits. Each is a discount that does not appear in the discount field.

## What goes wrong in practice

Three failures recur, and each shows up in the evidence.

The first is speed. Everstage's 2026 survey of 195 VP-level revenue leaders in North America, a vendor-run and self-reported study, found that 47% of teams took three days or more to approve a pricing exception, and 40% still built quotes and configured pricing by hand. A slow approval chain does not stop discounting. It teaches sellers to ask for more than they need, so the approved number lands where they wanted.

The second is timing. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmark of 4.2 million opportunities reported that offering discounts early in the sales process was associated with a 39% lower win rate. The figure is from a vendor dataset and is a correlation, but it fits what buyers say: an early discount tells the buyer that the first price was a starting point, and invites a second round.

The third is that overrides become the norm. McKinsey's 2026 distribution work describes a building materials distributor whose sellers overrode system-generated prices in more than half of all transactions. Overrides fell by 80% once the firm fixed its product data. The lesson is that frequent overrides are often a signal that the price list is wrong, not that sellers are undisciplined.

There is also a forecasting link. Gartner's 2020 research on forecast confidence warned that inaccurate forecasts lead leaders to approve discounts they would normally reject. Discounts granted to rescue a quarter are the ones least likely to be reviewed.

## The rules: bands, rights and trades

A discount policy that works fits on one page. It sets bands, says who can approve each band, sets a turnaround time and lists the trades a seller should ask for in return.

| Discount band (off list or standard price) | Who approves | Turnaround | What must be recorded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Within standard band (for example up to 5%) | Seller | Immediate | Reason code |
| Above standard, below senior threshold | Sales manager | Same working day | Reason, the trade obtained, competing offer if any |
| Above senior threshold | Deal desk or revenue leader with finance | Two working days | Reason, trade, margin after discount, renewal price |
| Non-price concessions (free services, extended terms, price locks) | Same as the cash-equivalent band | As above | Cash-equivalent value, reason, trade |
| Below the floor | Named executive only | Two working days | Full case, expected outcome, review date |

The band thresholds are the firm's own decision and should be set from its margin structure, not copied. The point of the table is that each level has an owner, a clock and a record. The last row matters: a floor that anyone can breach with enough pressure is not a floor.

The second rule is give-get. Every concession above the standard band should buy something the firm values. Common trades are a longer term, upfront payment, a larger initial commitment, a case study or reference, a faster signature, or reduced scope. A discount with no trade attached is a price cut.

| Concession requested | Trade worth asking for | Why it is a fair exchange |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Higher discount on year one | Multi-year term at stepped prices | Lower year-one price is recovered over the term |
| Extended payment terms | Price at or near list | Terms cost the firm working capital, not margin |
| Free implementation days | Named reference or case study rights | Lowers the firm's future selling cost |
| Price lock on renewal | Larger committed volume | Locks in revenue as well as price |
| Discount for end-of-quarter signature | Signature date written into the approval | Makes the trade testable after the fact |

The third rule is speed. The turnaround times above are as important as the approval levels. A same-day answer removes the incentive to pad the request. McKinsey's distribution research recommends an override-rate threshold, enforced with execution data, alongside price floors and clear escalation paths for strategic accounts. That is the same idea: measure how often the rules are broken, and treat a rising rate as a signal to examine the rules.

> A discount with nothing traded for it is a price cut, and it should be approved as one.

## Learn from every exception

The approval chain decides each deal. The record decides whether the policy improves. Every exception above the standard band is a commercial decision with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome, which is the shape set out in [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/). Discount approvals were one of the decisions that piece singled out, because they recur weekly and their outcome is known within a sales cycle.

The field that matters most is the expected outcome. "Approved 18% to beat a competing quote" is a reason. "Approved 18% to beat a competing quote; expect renewal at list in year two" is a prediction, and it can be checked. The piece on [the field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) makes the case in general.

A quarterly review then asks four questions of the exception log. Which reason codes appear most often, and do they point to a list price that is wrong for a segment? Which sellers or managers approve most often, and are their deals renewing? Did the trades recorded actually happen: did the case study get written, did the multi-year customer stay? And what is the spread of realised prices for similar deals, the modern version of Marn and Rosiello's pocket price band?

If the same exception is granted for the same reason ten times in a quarter, it is no longer an exception. Change the band or the price, and record that decision too.

Illustrative example: a discount band that was wrong

Decision
:   Raise the standard discount band for one segment from 5% to 10%, and remove manager approval for that range.

Reason and owner
:   A quarter's exception log showed most deals in the segment approved at 8–10% against the same competitor, with no difference in renewal rates. Agreed by the revenue leader and finance; owned by the deal desk.

What changed
:   Approval volume fell and turnaround for the remaining exceptions shortened. The firm set a review for two quarters later to check realised price and renewal rates in the segment.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software and services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price moves profit more than volume.** A 1% average discount can cost around a tenth of operating profit, which justifies a written policy.
- **Speed is part of control.** Slow approvals teach sellers to pad requests; same-day answers remove the reason to.
- **Trade for every concession.** If nothing is given in return, approve it as a price cut.
- **Read the exception log quarterly.** Repeated exceptions mean the band or the price is wrong.

Gateway card

### Before you publish a discount policy

- Discount bands set from the firm's own margin structure
- An approver and a turnaround time named for each band
- A floor that only one named executive can breach
- Non-price concessions converted to a cash-equivalent value
- A give-get list sellers can use in negotiation
- Reason, trade and expected outcome captured on every exception
- A quarterly review of the exception log booked with finance

## Common questions

### What is discount governance in sales?

Discount governance is the set of rules that decides who can approve which discounts, how fast, in exchange for what, and how each decision is recorded and reviewed.

### How much does a discount affect profit?

In Marn and Rosiello's analysis of 2,463 companies, a 1% change in realised price changed operating profit by about 11%, so even small average discounts have a large effect on profit.

### Who should approve sales discounts?

Most firms let sellers approve within a small standard band, sales managers approve the next band, and a deal desk or revenue leader with finance approve larger discounts, with a single executive for anything below the floor.

### What is a give-get in sales negotiation?

A give-get is a rule that every concession, such as a discount or free services, is exchanged for something of value to the seller, such as a longer term, upfront payment or a reference.

Export every deal from the last two quarters with list price, realised price and approver. Sort by the gap between them. If the largest gaps have no recorded reason, start by adding a mandatory reason field before changing any band.
